name: Begging the question
statement: Begging the question is offering as a premise the claim in dispute, and circular reasoning is the same fault spread over more steps rather than a separate one.
meaning: Aristotle's name for the fault was to en arche aiteisthai, asking for the thing at the start. It belonged to a game of question and answer in which a questioner had to win each premise from an answerer, and the foul was asking the answerer to grant the very point under dispute. Latin rendered aiteisthai as petitio and arche as principium, and English rendered petitio as beg and the disputed point as the question. Begging the question and circular reasoning are two names for one charge. Aristotle's own chapter on it covers the one-step version and the loop in which A is proved through B, B through C and C through A. Mill places reasoning in a circle inside petitio principii as a variety of it, and Hans Hansen's Stanford Encyclopedia entry calls circular reasoning the more involved version of begging the question. This atlas holds them as a single entry for that reason. Hansen also states the difficulty the charge carries. These arguments are not faulted for invalidity, so they are not condemned as non sequiturs like most of the core fallacies, and what is wrong with them has to be an epistemic complaint rather than a logical one.

origin.note: 'Circular reasoning' is the first experiment on the charge, and Rips writes that there appears to be no prior empirical research on the topic despite its importance in philosophy and rhetoric. The idea is far older and is Aristotle's. Sophistical Refutations chapter 5 lists seven fallacies outside language, the fifth being to en arche lambanein, and chapter 6 says these arise in as many ways as it is possible to ex arches aiteisthai. Prior Analytics II.16 gives what Topics VIII.13 calls the account according to truth. The Greek text used here places that chapter between the Bekker markers 64b and 65a. The Topics chapter gives the account according to reputable opinion, and counts five ways of appearing to beg the original point. Both the Latin petitio principii and the English phrase are later. Merriam-Webster dates 'beg the question' to 1581 in the sense of assuming what is at issue, and Mark Liberman quotes the Oxford English Dictionary's earliest citation as W. Clarke in 1581, 'I say this is still to begge the question'.

evidence: The textual record and the experimental record answer different questions. On the text, Aristotle's Prior Analytics II.16 opens by saying that begging the original point is, taken in general, a failure to demonstrate what was proposed, and that this happens in many ways. His test is whether someone tries to prove through itself what is not knowable through itself. The chapter then gives the multi-step case, where A is shown through B, B through C, and C is of a kind to be shown through A, and remarks that those who reason so end up proving A through A. His illustration is people who think they are drawing parallel lines. Topics VIII.13 counts five ways of appearing to beg the original point. The plainest is to ask outright for the thing that has to be shown, which he says is hard to conceal except where synonyms are involved, or where a name and its account signify the same. Mill, in Book V chapter VII of A System of Logic, files the fallacy under Fallacies of Confusion and names it 'Petitio Principii, or begging the question; including the more complex and not uncommon variety of it, which is termed Reasoning in a Circle'. He quotes Whately's definition, that the premise 'either appears manifestly to be the same as the conclusion, or is actually proved from the conclusion, or is such as would naturally and properly so be proved'. Mill adds that since every case where a conclusion provable only from certain premises is used to prove those premises is a case of petitio principii, the fallacy 'includes a very great proportion of all incorrect reasoning'. His examples are the scholastic argument that the mind thinks always because the essence of the mind is to think, and Moliere's physician explaining that opium sends people to sleep because it contains a dormitive virtue. On the experiments, Rips ran three studies on Northwestern undergraduates, each showing scripted two-person dialogues in which a proponent makes a target claim, the opponent acknowledges, queries or denies it, and the proponent finishes with a verbatim repetition, a paraphrase, or a new statement. One group ranked the final line for circularity, another for reasonableness, and no definition of either word was supplied. Experiment 1 used 60 participants, 30 per condition, on 20 topics with nine versions each. Ranks ran from 1 for most circular or least reasonable to 9 for the opposite. In the circularity condition new statements averaged 6.28, paraphrases 5.23 and repetitions 3.49; in the reasonableness condition 6.40, 5.32 and 3.27, with F1(2, 116) = 98.52, p < .0001 by participants and F2(2, 38) = 249.54, p < .0001 by schema. Experiment 2a, 60 participants, added a structural manipulation. When the opponent's penultimate question continued the same line of justification the argument was one-branch, and when it opened a new one the repeated claim no longer supported itself. Mean ranks on a 1 to 6 scale were 3.35 for one-branch and 3.65 for two-branch items, F1(1, 58) = 5.68, p < .05. That difference came almost entirely from the circularity group, whose means were 3.05 and 3.95, while the reasonableness group ran weakly the other way at 3.65 and 3.35, giving an interaction at F1(1, 58) = 22.46, p < .0001. Experiment 2b repeated the design with 80 participants rating rather than ranking. Circularity ratings tracked structure, 3.37 against 3.63, and ignored the opponent entirely: 3.50 after an acknowledgment, 3.52 after a query and 3.47 after a denial, both F values below 1. Reasonableness ratings did the reverse, 3.75, 3.68 and 3.39, F1(2, 78) = 15.25, p < .0001. Rips reads the pattern as two things coming apart. What people call circular depends on the shape of the proponent's own argument, and what they call reasonable depends on whether the audience had granted the claim, so the structurally circular arguments and the pragmatically defective ones only partly overlap. A preliminary study of his supplies the plainest fact about the phrase: asked what 'begging the question' means, 8 of 24 participants answered that they did not know, against 1 of 24 asked the same about circularity. Children have been tested separately. Baum, Danovitch and Keil gave 17 kindergarteners, mean age 5 years 8 months, nine phenomena with three explanations each, a short circular one, a long circular one and a noncircular one of matched length. The noncircular explanation was chosen 52.29% of the time against a chance rate of 33.33%, t(16) = 6.06, p < .0001, the short circular one 16.99%, and the long circular one at chance. A pilot of 27 adults chose the noncircular explanation 95% of the time. Their second experiment dropped the short circular option and tested 19 kindergarteners, 24 second graders and 17 fourth graders. Noncircular choice ran at 49.71%, 67.13% and 84.97%, F(2, 59) = 21.197, p < .001, with every pairwise gap holding. Kindergarteners were at chance, which is below their own performance in the first experiment, and the authors read the drop as an effect of removing the blatant option that had made the others salient. Mercier, Bernard and Clement then put the same contrast to preschoolers as testimony rather than explanation. Two characters disagree about which way a dog went, one saying 'because I've seen him go in this direction' and the other 'because he went in this direction'. Three-, 4- and 5-year-olds all favoured the perceptual argument. The same paper reports that 4- and 5-year-olds, though not 3-year-olds and not adults, preferred a claim backed by the circular argument over a claim backed by nothing, which the authors attribute to a heuristic reading of an argument as a cue to dominance. Hruschka and Appel taught five informal fallacies including begging the question to one arm of a 116-person experiment and the topic of fake news to the other. Learning the fallacies improved fallacy identification a week later, and both arms discriminated real from fake news equally well. Hahn and Oaksford's Psychological Review paper reports experiments on three fallacies, one of them 'the circular argument or petitio principii', testing whether rated strength moves with the factors a Bayesian account predicts. That paper is closed and was not obtained here, and nothing on this page rests on it.

replication.headline: The finding that has been repeated is that people prefer a non-circular argument to a circular one, in Swiss, Guatemalan Maya and Japanese preschoolers using the same two-character task. Rips's adult result, that judgements of circularity ignore whether the audience had granted the claim, has not been repeated by another group.
replication.detail: Mercier and colleagues ran the Swiss task on Japanese 5-year-olds twice. Experiment 1, 28 children with a mean age of 65.1 months, gave 61.9% choice of the perceptual argument over three trials, which was a trend rather than a result, Z = 1.85, p = .063. First-trial choice was 71%, or 20 of 28, and third-trial choice 46%, and the authors attribute the decline to repetition of the trials and to a Japanese sentence-final particle marking confidence in both statements. Experiment 3 used one trial, prerecorded voices and wording stripped of that particle, on 41 fresh children with a mean age of 65.6 months. Choice of the perceptual argument was 78%, 32 of 41, p < .01 by binomial test, which the paper reports as replicating both the Swiss and the Maya results. Neither cross-cultural comparison was reliable: against the Swiss children 78% versus 57.1%, chi-square(1, N = 69) = 3.43, p = .064, and against the Maya children 78% versus 72.7%, chi-square(1, N = 74) = .28, p = .59. Experiment 2, on 25 Japanese undergraduates, validated the stimuli at 88% and 96%. The Maya arm is Castelain, Bernard, Van der Henst and Mercier. Their abstract reports that 4- to 6-year-olds from a traditional Maya population endorsed the testimony supported by a strong argument over that supported by a weak one, and that argument quality overrode a dominance cue. The adult work has no independent repetition. Rips's own Experiments 2a and 2b are one design run twice by one group, and they disagree about the opponent's replies. The ranking version made circularity judgements sensitive to whether the claim had been denied and the rating version did not. Rips attributes the difference to the pressure a forced ranking puts on participants to discriminate.

study.cite: Mercier, H., Sudo, M., Castelain, T., Bernard, S., & Matsui, T. (2017). Japanese preschoolers' evaluation of circular and non-circular arguments. European Journal of Developmental Psychology, 15(5), 493-505. Experiment 3, n = 41.

limits: The search for experimental work covered Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar and general web search, pairing circularity, begging the question and petitio principii with terms for experiments, judgements and replication. Europe PMC returns 42 records for 'begging the question' with 'fallacy' and an experimental term, and the only experiment among them is Hruschka and Appel's, which teaches the fallacy rather than testing it. Weinstock, Neuman and Glassner's programme on identifying informal fallacies looks like the nearest fit and is not: their own review in Informal Logic, read in full, covers ad ignorantiam, ad hominem and ad populum and mentions circularity nowhere. On self-sealing and unfalsifiable claims the nearest work found is Friesen, Campbell and Kay in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. It is closed, has no open location at Unpaywall and no PubMed abstract, and was not obtained, so nothing is claimed from it here. Hahn and Oaksford's 2007 Psychological Review paper is the one that matters most and could not be read. Unpaywall returns no open location, the Birkbeck and Cardiff repositories hold metadata without full text, and the 2005 conference version at the Helsinki proceedings site returns 503. Only its abstract, read at Birkbeck, is used, and no figure from it appears above. The 2014 Swiss experiment was also not obtained. Its design and conclusions come from its PubMed abstract and from the 2017 paper's description. The 57.1% attributed to Swiss 5-year-olds is the 2017 paper's report of that figure rather than a figure read in the original. The Castelain Maya paper was read as its PubMed abstract only. The children's studies are small: 17, 19, 24 and 17 participants in Baum's cells, 28 and 41 in the Japanese ones. Rips's three studies all used introductory psychology undergraduates at one university, and his ranking measure forces a discrimination that a rating measure does not, which is the difference his own two versions turn on. Sparkes's two-page note in the Journal of the History of Ideas is behind JSTOR and was not obtained. Its argument and the 1577 quotations attached to it are quoted here from Mark Liberman's Language Log post, which reproduces them. The sixteenth-century texts themselves were not consulted. The claim that Boethius produced the Latin phrase appears in secondary summaries and no source carrying it was read, so this page does not say who made the translation. Aristotle was read in Greek at Greek Wikisource, which transcribes an edition it names but is not a critical text, and the phrases quoted were found in two separate works there rather than in one.
misreadings: The largest error is now the ordinary meaning. Merriam-Webster gives 'to elicit a question logically as a reaction or response' as sense 1 and the fallacy as sense 2, and dates the phrase to 1581 in sense 2. Rips recorded the drift in 2002, writing that in recent usage the phrase has come to mean something more like raising the question or leaving the question open. Liberman counted it in 2010: of the first 20 hits for 'beg the question' in the New York Times index, 15 meant 'raise the question', and four of the remaining five were columns complaining about the misuse. A second error is the story usually told to explain the first, that 'beg the question' is a bungled translation. Sparkes argued in 1966 that it is a literal description of a move in disputation. A disputant who asserts a premise is asking his opponent to grant it, and one who asserts the conclusion as a premise is asking to be granted the thing whose truth was in question. On that reading 'beg' and 'question' both carried their sixteenth-century senses correctly and it is modern English that moved. The third error is to treat circularity as a formal defect. Mill states the opposite in Book II chapter III of A System of Logic: 'It must be granted that in every syllogism, considered as an argument to prove the conclusion, there is a petitio principii.' All men are mortal cannot be known unless Socrates's mortality is already known, so a valid deduction that adds nothing to its premises is the ordinary case and not the fallacy. Hansen's survey records the consequence, that Whately invented a category of non-logical fallacies to hold begging the question because it is not an invalid form, and that a definition of fallacy resting on invalidity is too narrow to catch it. The fourth error is to file circular reasoning as a separate fallacy from begging the question. Aristotle, Mill and Hansen all treat the circle as a version of the one charge, and English Wikipedia's two articles drew 164,964 and 82,273 views in 2025 by the Wikimedia pageviews API for what those authors describe as one thing. Rips is the qualification: his participants judged structural circles circular whether or not the audience objected, and judged unreasonable the arguments the audience had refused, so the two classes overlap only in part, which he says supports those who want the distinction drawn. The last error is to think the accusation settles anything. Rips prints a case in which a Census Bureau researcher accused him of begging the question, records his own protest that there was independent evidence, and observes that charging others with question-begging is an intermural sport.

Source for circular reasoning being the more involved version of begging the question, for Whately's category of non-logical fallacies, and for the claim that a fallacy definition resting on invalidity is too narrow to catch it.

Mill, J. S. A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive, Book V chapter VII, Fallacies of Confusion. Read at English Wikisource. Source for petitio principii including reasoning in a circle as a variety of it, for Whately's definition as Mill quotes it, and for the Moliere and essence-of-mind examples.

Mill, J. S. A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive, Book II chapter III, Of the Functions and Logical Value of the Syllogism. Read at English Wikisource. Source for the sentence that every syllogism contains a petitio principii.

Aristotle, Prior Analytics, Book 2, chapter 16, in Greek at Greek Wikisource. Source for the phrases to en arche aiteisthai and to ex arches aiteisthai, for the test of proving through itself what is not knowable through itself, for the A through B through C loop and for the parallel-lines illustration.

Aristotle, Topics, Book 8, chapter 13, in Greek at Greek Wikisource. Source for the five ways of appearing to beg the original point and for Aristotle's remark that the account according to truth is in the Analytics and the account according to opinion is given there.
Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations, chapters 5 and 6, in Greek at Greek Wikisource. Source for the list of seven fallacies outside language with to en arche lambanein fifth.

Source for the Oxford English Dictionary citation list, for Schreiber's literal renderings of the Greek, for Liddell and Scott's logical sense of aiteo, for the New York Times count, and for the Sparkes argument. All of those are quoted at one remove through this post.

Sparkes, A. W. (1966). 'Begging the Question'. Journal of the History of Ideas, 27(3), 462. Not obtained; behind JSTOR. The record was verified at Crossref and the argument is quoted through Language Log.
